title: Automation & Endpoints
subtitle: Sysmon, auditd, the media storage server, Ansible, the Python automation engine, and the full ransomware containment playbook.

intro.text: This is everything underneath the Wazuh alert: the endpoint agents feeding it telemetry, the simulated media server it protects, and the automation chain that actually reacts when rule 100200 fires. Most of this lives under BCE-RTL-SOC-LAB/ in the repository — the deliverable artifacts, not just narrative.

blocks.text: Sysmon (Microsoft Sysinternals) is the Windows-side equivalent of auditd: deep process, network and registry telemetry that goes far beyond default Windows Event Logs. It's what feeds the T1548.003/T1078 MITRE-mapped alerts referenced throughout the Wazuh page.

items: Check for a pre-existing install first — relevant for cloned/reused VMs.
Download only from the official Microsoft Sysinternals source.
Install with a curated, MITRE ATT&CK-mapped community config (SwiftOnSecurity or olafhartong/sysmon-modular) rather than the sparse default one.
Wire the Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational and PowerShell-Operational channels into the Wazuh agent's ossec.conf.
Validate on the dashboard.

blocks.title: A documented, expected false positive
blocks.text: Rule 92910 ("VBoxService accessing Explorer — possible process injection") fires routinely on VirtualBox guests. It's a real, benign behavior of the Guest Additions service — a genuine example of the kind of tuning decision every SOC has to make, not a bug to chase.

The Linux Audit Framework watches syscalls and file access at the kernel level — identity changes, privilege escalation, SSH config changes, and (extended for this lab) mass file operations that look like ransomware behavior.
Base watch rules

blocks.code:
-w /etc/passwd -p wa -k identity
-w /etc/group -p wa -k identity
-w /etc/shadow -p wa -k identity
-w /etc/sudoers -p wa -k privilege
-w /etc/ssh/sshd_config -p wa -k sshd_config

blocks.text: Extended, ransomware-relevant rules built for this lab

items: Mass file delete/rename detection via syscall auditing (unlink, unlinkat, rename, renameat)
Kernel-module load/unload — a rootkit indicator
setuid/setgid privilege escalation
The /srv/media watch used directly by the media-server phase
Cron persistence paths and SSH authorized_keys changes
mount/umount monitoring — exfiltration via external media

blocks.title: A gotcha that costs a false negative on the first test, every time
blocks.text: The first `touch` on a monitored file, before realtime FIM is actually enabled, only becomes part of the baseline — it does not trigger an alert. The file has to be touched again after the agent restart to see the real detection. Also: Wazuh's default scan cycle for /etc is 12 hours, far too slow for live detection — realtime FIM has to be explicitly enabled.
Turns a connected Linux endpoint into the lab's actual protected asset — the centerpiece of the whole "ransomware isolation in media storage networks" premise.

items: Samba share ([MediaLab], valid users = @mediaops) simulating how a real ingest/transcode/playout pipeline would mount storage
UFW configured least-privilege, LAN-only
Realtime FIM enabled on /srv/media in ossec.conf (report_changes="yes" to capture diffs) plus a matching auditd watch rule (-w /srv/media -p wa -k media_changes)
Populated with 100 dummy files, then tested with a real rename to confirm a rule-553 alert appears within seconds

blocks.text: This exact folder structure — ingest → live → archive → backup → quarantine — is the concrete stand-in for a broadcaster's real pipeline, and every automation script in this lab targets it specifically.

A dedicated tree at /opt/soc-automation/{bin,logs,reports}, its own virtualenv, kept deliberately separate from the OS and Wazuh's own Python — a real lesson about not creating dependency conflicts with a running SIEM.
The scripts, one per distinct side effect

rows: The orchestrator — reads the triggering Wazuh alert from stdin, generates one microsecond-resolution incident_id, and calls the three scripts below under it
Network-level containment — pushes iptables DROP rules in both directions on the virtual router, tagged with the incident ID for later reversal
Quarantines the affected transcode-worker container and brings up a clean replacement, so playout never fully drops
Writes a structured JSON incident report using the file hash already computed by Wazuh's own FIM (syscheck.sha256_after) — the manager has no filesystem access to the agent to hash it itself
The experimental-evaluation harness — triggers a rename over SSH and measures wall-clock time to a new forensic report, avoiding human reaction time contamination

blocks.title: The REPORT_ONLY safety gate
blocks.text: Every script defaults to REPORT_ONLY = True — it logs exactly what it would do ("would isolate agent X", "would fail over container Y") without actually executing it. The golden rule followed throughout: never flip it to live-action mode until validated across many real and simulated events with zero false positives. A false positive here means an automated, unattended disconnection of a real node.
Two real bugs found building this

items: forensic_alert.py initially returned "unavailable" for every file hash — it was trying to read a file that only exists on the agent's disk, from the manager, which has no such access. Fixed by consuming the hash Wazuh's FIM had already computed, instead of re-reading the file.

A large paste inside nano silently dropped the trailing `if __name__ == "__main__":` block from an Active Response script. wazuh-execd logged "command dispatched" successfully, and the script itself exited 0 with zero output — the exact signature of a script that only defines functions and never calls any of them.

blocks.code:
[linux_endpoints]
victim-linux ansible_user=tales ansible_host=192.168.178.177
tales-desktop ansible_user=tales ansible_host=192.168.178.92
kali-vm ansible_user=kali ansible_host=192.168.178.156

blocks.title: The passphrase race condition
blocks.text: If the SSH private key has a passphrase, Ansible's parallel connections to multiple hosts race for the same one interactive passphrase prompt and fail unpredictably. Fixed by unlocking the key once via ssh-agent/ssh-add before running any Ansible command — after that, every parallel connection reuses the already-unlocked agent.

The gap between host-local firewalling (UFW, on soc-server itself) and the target role's requirement to update actual network equipment — firewall, switch, router — via an API. Since real production network hardware isn't practical to practice against, a virtual topology fills the gap: one FRRouting virtual router (router1), connected to two storage nodes (storage-a, storage-b).

blocks.title: NETCONF was the plan — until it wasn't
blocks.text: The original design used NAPALM/NETCONF to manage the virtual router programmatically, matching what real network-equipment APIs look like. The FRR image used doesn't run an SSH server at all, ruling that out entirely. The pragmatic substitute: docker exec as the router's "management API" — functionally equivalent for demonstrating programmatic, non-manual network control, which is what mattered for the isolation use case. Cisco DevNet Sandbox is noted as a free option for practicing real NETCONF/RESTCONF later.

This is exactly what isolate_node.py uses under the hood: bidirectional iptables DROP rules, tagged with the incident ID, pushed onto the virtual router via docker exec, with a documented, symmetric reversal command set.

sections.title: The ransomware containment playbook, end to end

blocks.text: The full chain, trigger to resolution — this is the actual deliverable the internship posting was preparing for.

items: Trigger: Wazuh rule 100200 (level 12) fires on FIM events 550/553/554 under /srv/media. A single rename produces two FIM events (delete + add), both independently handled.
Isolate: network-level containment of the affected agent, iptables DROP both directions, tagged with the shared incident ID.
Failover: the affected transcode-worker container is quarantined (renamed, never deleted — inspectable and restorable) and a clean replacement is brought up, so "playout" never fully drops.
Forensic report: a structured JSON incident record is written, using the FIM-computed hash rather than re-reading the file.

Reversal (tested end to end): tagged iptables rules removed by incident ID; the quarantined container is restorable. Validated with a full backup/restore cycle — 100 files renamed in bulk, then restored from a tar.gz snapshot taken immediately before the simulated attack.

blocks.title: The non-negotiable safety rule
blocks.text: REPORT_ONLY stayed True for every single test run described anywhere on this site. Flipping it to live-action mode is a decision that was never made lightly, because a false positive here means an automated, unattended disconnection of a real live media node.

Gathered with measure_latency.py, purpose-built to avoid contaminating results with human reaction time. An earlier manual-trigger attempt returned 18.05s and was discarded — it was measuring terminal-switching speed, not the pipeline.
Single-event latency (n=10)

The distribution is notably bimodal — roughly half the runs cluster near 1s, half near 4s — most likely reflecting wazuh-analysisd's internal processing cycle: some events get picked up almost immediately, others wait for the next cycle.
Burst test — 100 simultaneous file renames

items: Pure local batch rename: 91 ms.
Time for the Wazuh manager to fully process the resulting FIM events: ~2m45s, at roughly 1 event/second sustained.
Total alerts generated: 300, not the 200 initially expected — the extra 100 were backlogged "file added" events from the original test-file creation, queued behind the burst.
System load stayed under 1.5 throughout — confirming the bottleneck was wazuh-analysisd/syscheckd processing throughput on 2-core hardware, not CPU saturation.

blocks.title: The most significant bug found in the whole project
blocks.text: Active Response fired roughly 300 times, but only about 100 unique forensic reports were written. Root cause: incident_id used 1-second timestamp resolution, so multiple genuinely distinct events landed on the same ID within the same second, and each forensic_alert.py invocation silently overwrote the prior JSON report for that ID — real evidence loss, at exactly the moment (a mass attack) it would matter most. Fixed with microsecond-resolution IDs, generated once by the orchestrator and passed down to every downstream script instead of each one generating its own. Re-validated with a 20-file batch: zero collisions.

Takeaway: single-event latency, in the low single digits of seconds, is fast enough to catch and contain a live-signal-threatening event well within a realistic requirement. The burst test's throughput ceiling and the incident-ID bug are the more interesting engineering-maturity findings — what breaks under a realistic multi-file attack, not just the single-file happy path.
A real report generated by forensic_alert.py during testing — the schema every downstream script produces and consumes, designed once and reused everywhere:

blocks.code:
{
  "incident_id": "INC-20260802-091550",
  "detected_utc": "2026-08-02T09:15:50.947161+00:00",
  "detecting_host": "soc-server",
  "source_ip": "192.168.178.177",
  "affected_path": "/srv/media/ingest/teste_diagnostico4.txt",
  "file_sha256": "e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855",
  "triggering_rule_id": "100200",
  "action_taken": "isolate+failover (report-only)",
  "playout_impact": "none",
  "status": "open",
  "next_steps": "review in SOC dashboard, confirm containment, RCA"
}

blocks.text: The playout_impact field is deliberate: it directly tracks the target role's central non-functional requirement — whether the live broadcast signal was affected — and is always "none" by design, since failover keeps a worker running throughout.

Wazuh agent (scheduled FIM only — documented limitation)

blocks.text: Used whenever a VM is reinstalled or recreated and needs to re-register — or when a machine is permanently retired.

items: Identify the stale agent via agent_control -l.
Remove the old manager-side registration first — via the dashboard (Agents management → Delete) or manage_agents CLI — before generating a new install command on the same machine.
If the machine is being retired entirely, fully uninstall the agent locally as well.

blocks.text: Skipping the removal step before reinstalling on the same machine produces "Agent key already in use" — a real, repeatable error hit on almost every reused VM in this lab.
